description: We are a multidisciplinary trio uniting physics, computer science, and creative problem-solving for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. By pairing deep scientific principles with scalable software engineering, we transform complex NASA open data into practical, innovative solutions for Earth and space.
summary: Last Transmission is an interactive web story that lets children hear the last words of twelve NASA machines left on the Moon, Mars and deep space. As you scroll, each machine’s signal fades, its photo loses colour, and a live silence clock counts the time since it went quiet. Each machine speaks in the first person, and a quick guess tests what you learned. Built for ages 9 to 14 with plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, it is accessible, works offline and uses only NASA-checked facts. Its aim is simple: twelve machines went quiet, but none of them are forgotten.
details:
What it does and how it works
Last Transmission is an interactive web story about twelve NASA machines left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space, listed in the order they went quiet, from 1967 to 2024. As you scroll through each machine’s chapter, a signal meter falls from 100% to 0%, the machine’s name thins out and its photo slowly loses colour. Each machine speaks in the first person, typed out like a radio message. A live “silence clock” counts the years, days and seconds since its last signal. At the end of each chapter, a one-question quick guess checks what you just read, and the page tracks how many signals you’ve heard and how many guesses you got right.

Benefits
It turns hardware that is easy to forget into characters children care about, while teaching real NASA science. Every date and fact is checked against NASA sources, and only the voices are imagined. The site is free, needs no sign-up, and opens with one double-click.

Intended impact
We want children to feel the silence first, then learn what each machine discovered, so that none of these explorers is forgotten. The project shows that a mission’s story doesn’t end when the signal does.

Tools and technology
The site is plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no libraries and no build step. It is a single file, hosted on Netlify. Photos come from NASA’s Image and Video Library, and facts come from NASA’s spacecraft archive (NSSDCA) and NASA Science mission pages. All photos are credited, and illustrations are labelled as illustrations.

Creativity
Instead of listing facts, we let the machines speak, and we made the loss of signal something you can see and feel through the meter, the fading photo and the silence clock. The quick guess turns reading into play.

Factors we considered

  • Audience: school-age explorers aged 9 to 14, in plain, friendly language, though anyone curious can enjoy it.
  • Accessibility: a hyperlegible font, keyboard and screen-reader support, and a reduced-motion mode.
  • Accuracy: all facts are checked against NASA sources, the imagined voices are clearly labelled, and we state that NASA does not endorse the project.
  • Simplicity: a single file that works offline, so any school or home can use it.
